body.heading: Writing on radio waves
paragraphs: Wi-Fi carries data on radio waves, the same kind of energy as light but with much longer wavelengths, in bands around 2.4 and 5 billion cycles per second. To send information, the transmitter tweaks the wave — its strength, timing or phase — in patterns that stand for ones and zeros.

The receiving device watches for those patterns and translates them back into data. Both sides switch between sending and listening many times a second, following shared rules — the Wi-Fi standards — so that laptops, phones and routers from different makers understand each other.

body.heading: Why walls and distance matter
paragraphs: Radio waves at these frequencies pass through wood, plaster and glass reasonably well, but brick, concrete and metal weaken or reflect them. Every wall between you and the router dims the signal, like a voice through closed doors.

The 2.4 gigahertz band travels farther and penetrates walls better; the 5 gigahertz band offers more room and higher speeds but fades sooner. Routers use both, steering devices to whichever serves them best — speed near the router, reach far from it.

body.heading: A crowded room, politely shared
paragraphs: Radio space is shared with neighbours' networks, baby monitors and microwave ovens, which leak a little energy in the same 2.4 band. Wi-Fi handles the crowd like polite conversation: each device listens before speaking and waits if someone else is mid-sentence.

The newest standards squeeze more data into each transmission by packing the wave's changes more densely — hundreds of millions of bits per second through thin air. All of it rides on energy you cannot see, passing through you harmlessly every day. It is, in effect, radio with manners.
